blocks.text: Ezra's response to the report of intermarriage among the returned exiles begins with profound grief. In prayer before the house of God, Ezra makes confession of the community's transgression, and his visible mourning draws a great assembly of men, women, and children who weep together. This collective emotional response marks the community's acknowledgment that covenant boundaries have been breached.

Shecaniah articulates both the reality of transgression and a path forward: the people have married foreign women, yet hope remains through a covenant to dissolve these unions according to law. Ezra accepts leadership of this resolution, administering oaths binding the chief priests, Levites, and all Israel to implement the dissolution process. The oath-taking represents a formal commitment across all levels of the community's leadership structure.

The investigation proceeds systematically through proclamation: all exiles must gather in Jerusalem within three days or face forfeiture and expulsion. The assembled crowd represents the full scope of the exile community—priests, Levites, and laymen from Judah and Benjamin—all subject to examination. Ezra's address to the trembling assembly reiterates the central transgression: marriages to foreign women threaten to compound Israel's guilt.
